draft.briefing: Hey, you're in Vagamon! This hill station in the Western Ghats sat largely unexplored for centuries, until tea planters made it known in 1926. Now it even has the Vagamon glass bridge, the longest cantilever glass bridge in India.
draft.hungryLine: My notes don't name any eateries up here, but if you're in Kerala for Onam, look out for the Onasadya, the big festival feast.

moodReplies.show-me-around: Walk out on the Vagamon glass bridge, then go up to Kurisumala Ashram, the Trappist monastery founded here in 1955.
moodReplies.somewhere-to-chill: Find a quiet slope among the tea plantations and enjoy the natural setting Vagamon is known for.
moodReplies.surprise-me: In 1963, architect Laurie Baker and Dr. Elizabeth Baker set up a hospital at Kurishumala to care for tea-plantation workers in these hills.

tips.title: Bring rain gear.
tips.body: Kerala gets rain for at least 7-8 months a year, so the hills here are often wet.

tips.title: Know your palli.
tips.body: In Kerala both mosques and churches are called palli, so ask which one if you're getting directions.

story.title: Unexplored hills
story.body: Vagamon sat on the border of what are now Kottayam and Idukki districts, largely unexplored. The British had plantations here, but few people knew it.

story.title: Tea makes it known
story.body: Walter Duncan and Company started tea plantations in 1926, and Vagamon became well known. More plantations followed in the 1930s.

story.title: New settlers
story.body: People from Travancore and Madras moved up to Vagamon. After Kerala State was formed, people came from all over Kerala too.

story.title: The monastery
story.body: Kurisumala Ashram, a Trappist monastery, was founded in Vagamon in 1955.

story.title: A hospital for the hills
story.body: Dr. Elizabeth Baker and architect Laurie Baker set up a hospital and rural service centre at Kurishumala. It served tea-plantation workers and rural families across the Idukki hills.
